newsitem.title: UK: MINOR METALS - Slow, but business set to flourish.
newsitem.headline: MINOR METALS - Slow, but business set to flourish.

text.p: Business in some of the minor metal markets showed some signs of increased activity as traders turned their attention to fourth quarter consumer requirements following the traditionally slow summer period .

Market talk focused on a recent Ukrainian germanium metal tender which left Western traders nervous of further price gyrations near-term. Elsewhere Russian cobalt held recent gains. Referring to the minor metals in general, one trader commented, "Pockets of activity are emerging...business will bloom by the end of September.
Traders said 6-1/2 tonnes of stockpiled Ukrainian germanium metal was believed to be sold at a tender, but they were unable to give a firm indication of what price the transaction was concluded at.

Several suggested the price paid by three companies at the tender was well below current market levels. The material is expected to filter on to the market in mid-September. Opinions remained divided on what impact the tender would have to the germanium market as a whole.
Several argued that the sale had already been factored into the market and that 6-1/2 tonnes could be absorbed by the booming fibre optics industry.
"It can be absorbed as long as it is handled correctly," one trader said.
But another aired caution, "It is likely to cause a shock wave and may tempt longs to liquidate further...I can see prices slipping further."
Cobalt continued its upward spiral, with several traders forecasting a gain by $2 for Russian material over current levels near-term. Others said it could possibly reach $28 by the end of 1996.

Scrap prices have picked up over the last few weeks, which is a indication of a tight market, traders said. From levels of around $17 a lb, scrap now stand around $19.50/20.50 lb for 70/80 percent nickel-bearing residues and scrap.
One trader said major producer Inco have raised their price to $24.50, while Falconbridge material remains very tight.
This should underpin the market during the UK Farnborough Air Show week, with traders noting brisk orders coming through in the aerospace sector.

Also, Zambia and Zaire are both facing problems from the fall-out of the 30-percent price decline in copper and associated margin calls. Cobalt that is held as collateral by Western banks may well be released, the traders added.
But with these factors quickly fading into the background many traders are looking at tight market fundamentals which are pointing to higher levels.
Increased industrial third and fourth quarter demand from China and India and restricted Russian supplies hold the key to higher levels, traders explained.
A halt of refined cobalt production at Severonickel in Russia continues to squeeze supplies.
Global cobalt stocks in Africa, Rotterdam and Antwerp at below 2,000 tonnes are at the lowest since 1977, according to a Commodities Research Unit (CRU) estimate.
Traders now see few dampening influences on the market, though several were quick to note increased production from Zambia and Canada's Falconbridge.
Mercury firmed slightly due to slow shipments from Russia and Spain. Chinese demand was underpinning the market.

Bismuth remained in the doldrums, although consumer covering was expected to emerge near-term. Cadium firmed slightly on speculative buying and light enquiries from consumers covering their fouther quarter needs.
Traders noted news that producer Norsk Hydro had cut its price for European pure magnesium to 6.30 marks per kilogramme from $6.55 marks. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 8075
